sentences.text: Udanoceratops is a large leptoceratopsid dinosaur estimated to reach nearly 4 meters in length and weigh about 700 kilograms.
Its skull was significantly larger and taller than those of other leptoceratopsids and protoceratopsids, measuring between 60 and 70 centimeters in length.
The holotype preserves a near-complete skull, several vertebrae, shoulder bones, hip bones, and some limb bones, with evidence suggesting it had nine cervical vertebrae.
Based on related taxa, the animal likely possessed nine thoracic, three lumbar, eight sacral, and between 38 and 50 caudal vertebrae.
This species holds the record as the largest known leptoceratopsid.
Researchers have proposed that the animal engaged in ritual head-swinging confrontations, likely between two males.
The teeth of Udanoceratops functioned only as cutting mechanisms.
The genus was first named and described by Russian paleontologist Sergei Kurzanov in 1992, with the type species being Udanoceratops tschizhovi.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as PIN 3907/11, was collected in the 1980s by the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition.
It was found at the Udan-Sayr locality in dark grey sandstones designated as Bed 2.
While some suggest Udanoceratops was semi-aquatic, its claw shape is more likely an adaptation for walking on soft substrates like sand dunes without sinking.
Bipedal running is unlikely; if it ran, it likely did so on all fours and was slower than smaller relatives.

Kurzanov suggested that the large skull was used in ritual head-swinging confrontations, though Gregory S. Paul argued in 2016 that a break on the holotype skull was caused by the beak of another individual rather than ritual combat.
It is placed within the Leptoceratopsidae, being the only Asian representative at the time alongside the North American Leptoceratops, Montanoceratops, and Prenoceratops.
Fossils are known from the Djadochta Formation in Mongolia, an area also famous for Protoceratops and Velociraptor, dating to the Campanian stage from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.

It is debated whether a large skull from the Bayan Mandahu Formation belongs to Udanoceratops; some researchers suspect it was misidentified as Protoceratops hellenikorhinus, and Łukasz Czepiński noted in 2020 that there are no specimens attributable to Udanoceratops from the Bayan Mandahu collections.
The status of a juvenile specimen, PIN 4046/11, is debated, with some studies considering it an indeterminate leptoceratopsid rather than Udanoceratops.
It is currently the largest named leptoceratopsid, though fragmentary remains from Kazakhstan might represent a similarly sized animal.
